title: Small cut or graze
problem: A small cut or scrape on the skin, for example from a kitchen knife, paper or a fall.
modern_guidance: Stop the bleeding with pressure, rinse the wound clean with water, and cover it with a clean plaster or dressing.
evidence_summary: Pressure, rinsing with clean water and a clean covering is standard first-aid advice from public health bodies such as the NHS.
how_to: Wash and dry your hands first.
Press on the cut with a clean folded cloth or bandage until it stops bleeding. Raise a hand or arm above heart level if you can.
Rinse the cut with clean tap or bottled water. Pat dry with clean gauze or cloth.
Clean the skin around it with soap and water, wiping away from the wound.
Cover with a plaster or sterile dressing. Keep it clean and dry and change it when needed.
what_to_avoid: Do not pull out anything stuck deep in the wound. Press around it and get help.
Do not pack the cut with powders, ash, coffee, or toothpaste.
Do not give aspirin to children under 16 for pain.
watch_for: Redness, swelling or pain that is getting worse after a day or two
Pus, or a bad smell from the wound
Feeling generally unwell or feverish
contraindications: People on blood-thinning medicines may bleed longer. Seek advice if bleeding is hard to control.
red_flags: Bleeding that does not slow after 10 minutes of firm pressure
Blood spurting from the wound
A deep cut, a gaping wound, or one longer than about 5 cm
An object stuck in the wound
Numbness or cannot move fingers or toes normally
when_to_seek_help: The wound has soil, pus or body fluids in it, or is still dirty after cleaning
It was caused by a human bite or a wild or stray animal
The cut is larger than about 5 cm, or on the face
Signs of infection: swelling, redness, increasing pain or pus

traditional_use.practice: Applying haldi (turmeric) powder to a fresh cut
traditional_use.note: Widely used in Indian homes. There is not enough good evidence that turmeric on a wound helps it heal.
traditional_use.safety: Loose powder can bring dirt into an open wound and may stain or irritate skin. Clean water and a clean dressing are the safer first step.

audience_notes.child: For children, keep the dressing on and check it daily. Get help if they will not let you clean it properly.
audience_notes.older_adult: Older skin tears more easily and heals slower. Check the wound daily for signs of infection.
audience_notes.infant: For a baby under 1, any cut that keeps bleeding or gapes should be seen by a doctor.

clarify.text: Does any of this apply to the cut?
clarify.text_hi: क्या इनमें से कुछ भी लागू होता है?

options.label: None of these: it is small and bleeding has slowed
options.label_hi: इनमें से कुछ नहीं: छोटा है, खून कम हो गया

options.label_hi: 10 मिनट दबाने पर भी खून बह रहा
options.reason: Bleeding that does not stop with 10 minutes of pressure needs urgent medical care.

options.reason: Deep or gaping cuts may need stitches or glue. Get medical care today.

options.label: Something is stuck in it
options.reason: Do not remove objects stuck in a wound. Press around it and get medical help.

options.label: Caused by an animal or human bite
options.label_hi: जानवर या इंसान के काटने से
options.reason: Bites need medical assessment. Wash with soap and running water for 15 minutes and get care today.

options.reason: Dirty wounds carry an infection and tetanus risk. Ask a doctor or pharmacist about tetanus protection.

title: Small burn or scald
problem: A small burn from a hot tawa, pressure cooker steam, hot oil, tea or an iron.
age_range: All ages (children and babies need extra care)
modern_guidance: Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible, then cover it loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy covering.
evidence_summary: Cooling with running water for 20 minutes is standard first-aid guidance. Creams, oils and butter are advised against.
how_to: Hold the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes. Start as soon as you can, ideally within 3 hours.
No running water? Use cool bottled water or a wet clean cloth.
Take off rings, bangles, watches or clothing near the burn, unless stuck to the skin.
Once cooled, lay cling film loosely over it. Do not wrap it tightly around a limb.
Keep the person warm otherwise, especially children. Cool the burn, not the whole body.
what_to_avoid: Do not put toothpaste, butter, ghee, oil, flour, or creams on the burn.
Do not use ice or ice water.
Do not burst blisters.
Do not use sticky plasters or fluffy cotton on the burn.
watch_for: Increasing pain, redness or swelling after a day or two
Pus or a bad smell
Fever
contraindications: Chemical and electrical burns are not covered here. They need emergency care.
red_flags: Burn larger than the palm of the hand of the person burned
Burn on the face, hands, feet, genitals, bottom, or over a joint
Deep burn: white, charred, leathery, or painless skin
Electrical or chemical burn
Any burn in a baby, or a burn with blistering in a young child
Breathing in smoke or steam, or a hoarse voice or cough after a fire
when_to_seek_help: Any of the red flags above: go to emergency care
You are not sure how serious it is
Signs of infection while it heals

traditional_use.practice: Toothpaste, ghee, butter or oil on a burn
traditional_use.note: Very common household advice. Public health guidance says not to put creams, oils or butter on burns.
traditional_use.safety: These trap heat, can cause infection and make the burn harder for a doctor to assess.

traditional_use.practice: Aloe vera gel on a healing minor burn
traditional_use.note: Some people use plain aloe vera once the burn has fully cooled and the skin is intact.
traditional_use.safety: Never as a replacement for 20 minutes of cool water. Do not use on broken skin or blisters. Stop if it irritates.

audience_notes.child: Children have thinner skin and burn more deeply. If the burn has blisters or is bigger than a coin, get it checked.
audience_notes.infant: Any burn on a baby should be seen by a doctor.
audience_notes.older_adult: Older skin burns more deeply and heals slower. Get larger or blistered burns checked.

not_for.reason: Any burn on a baby should be assessed by a doctor.

options.label_hi: इनमें से कुछ नहीं: छोटा, लाल और दर्द

options.reason: Burns in these areas need to be seen by a doctor.

options.reason: These can be signs of a deep burn. Get emergency care.

title: Bruise or bump
problem: A blue, purple or dark mark after bumping into something or a minor fall.
modern_guidance: Rest the area and apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling and pain. Most bruises fade on their own over one to two weeks.
evidence_summary: Cold compresses and rest are standard first-aid advice for bruises. Bruises normally fade without treatment.
how_to: Hold a cold pack or frozen peas wrapped in a cloth on the area for up to 20 minutes.
Rest and, if possible, raise the bruised part.
Repeat the cold pack a few times over the first day or two.
what_to_avoid: Do not put ice directly on skin.
Do not massage a fresh bruise hard.
watch_for: Swelling that keeps growing
Pain that is getting worse instead of better
Bruises that appear without any injury
contraindications: People on blood thinners bruise more easily and should mention unexplained bruises to their doctor.
red_flags: Bruise after a head injury with drowsiness, vomiting, confusion or severe headache
Cannot move or put weight on the injured part
Very large swelling or a deformed-looking limb
Unexplained bruising, especially with bleeding gums or nosebleeds
when_to_seek_help: Bruising appears for no reason or very easily
Pain and swelling are severe or not improving after a few days
Injury to the eye area or head

traditional_use.practice: Haldi (turmeric) lep on a bruise
traditional_use.note: Common household practice. Evidence that turmeric on the skin speeds healing of bruises is not established.
traditional_use.safety: Usually harmless on unbroken skin but can stain. Do not use on open wounds. Stop if the skin gets irritated.

audience_notes.child: A child with a bump on the head who is drowsy, vomits, or acts unusually needs urgent medical care.
audience_notes.older_adult: Falls in older adults can cause hidden injuries. Watch for new confusion or pain on walking.

options.reason: Watch closely for 24 hours after a head bump. Get urgent help for drowsiness, vomiting or confusion.

options.label: Yes, with vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or fainting
options.reason: These are warning signs after a head injury. Get emergency care now.

clarify.text: Can the injured part move and take weight normally?

options.label: No, or it looks out of shape
options.reason: This could be a fracture. Get it checked.

title: Blister
problem: A small bubble of fluid under the skin, usually from new shoes or rubbing.
modern_guidance: Leave the blister intact, keep it clean, and cover it with a soft or padded plaster. Most heal within a week.
evidence_summary: NHS guidance: do not burst blisters, keep them clean and covered, and avoid whatever caused the rubbing until healed.
how_to: Gently wash the area and pat it dry.
Cover with a soft plaster or padded dressing.
If it bursts on its own, let the fluid drain, do not peel the skin, and cover it.
Avoid the shoes or activity that caused it until it heals.
what_to_avoid: Do not burst it with a needle or pin.
Do not peel off the loose skin.
Do not pick at the edges.
watch_for: Yellow or green pus
Skin around it becoming hot, red or more painful
contraindications: People with diabetes or poor circulation should get foot blisters checked.
red_flags: Blisters from a burn, sunburn or allergic reaction
Blisters on the eyelids, mouth or genitals
Many blisters appearing for no reason
when_to_seek_help: The blister looks infected
It is very painful or keeps coming back
You have diabetes and the blister is on your foot

clarify.text: What caused the blister?

options.label: A burn or sunburn
options.reason: Blisters from burns are treated as burns. See the burn guide and get larger ones checked.

options.label: No clear reason, or many appeared
options.reason: Blisters that appear for no reason should be checked by a doctor.

title: Small splinter
problem: A small piece of wood, thorn or glass just under the surface of the skin.
modern_guidance: If the end is visible and shallow, clean the area and pull it out in the same direction it went in with clean tweezers, then wash and cover.
evidence_summary: Removal of shallow splinters with clean tweezers is common first-aid practice (St John Ambulance). We did not find a verified source page for exact steps, so this guide is marked for expert review.
how_to: Wash your hands and the skin with soap and water.
Clean tweezers with soap and hot water or an alcohol wipe.
Grip the visible end and pull it out gently at the same angle it went in.
Squeeze gently so a little blood flushes the wound, then wash and cover with a plaster.
what_to_avoid: Do not dig deep with a needle.
Do not try to remove glass or metal that is deep or near the eye.
watch_for: Redness, swelling, pus or throbbing over the next days
A piece left behind
contraindications: People with diabetes should get foot splinters checked.
red_flags: Splinter in or near the eye
Deeply embedded splinter, glass or metal
Splinter under a fingernail that cannot be reached
when_to_seek_help: You cannot get it out
Signs of infection
Tetanus protection may not be up to date and the object was dirty

source.supports: General first-aid reference (bruises, splinters, sprains).

title: Mosquito or insect bite
problem: An itchy or painful red bump from a mosquito, ant, bed bug or similar insect.
modern_guidance: Wash the bite with soap and water, hold a cold compress on it, and try not to scratch. Most bites settle within a few days.
evidence_summary: NHS guidance: wash the area, apply a cold compress, avoid scratching. A pharmacist can suggest anti-itch options.
how_to: Wash the area with soap and water.
Hold a cold compress (a cloth soaked in cold water, or ice wrapped in cloth) on it for at least 10 minutes.
Raise the area if it is swollen.
Keep nails short, especially for children, to avoid breaking the skin by scratching.
A pharmacist can suggest suitable anti-itch creams or antihistamines if the itch is bad.
what_to_avoid: Do not scratch: it can cause infection.
Do not apply kerosene, petrol or strong chemicals.
Do not use home remedies like bicarbonate of soda on the bite (NHS advises against it).
watch_for: Redness or swelling spreading over the next days
Pus, or feeling unwell
Fever in the days or week after mosquito bites
red_flags: Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat
Difficulty breathing or wheezing
Feeling faint, dizzy or confused after a bite or sting
High fever, severe body ache or pain behind the eyes in the days after mosquito bites (possible dengue or malaria)
when_to_seek_help: Symptoms are not improving after a few days, or are getting worse
Signs of infection, like pus or spreading redness
A fever in the days after being bitten, especially in monsoon
Bitten in the mouth or throat, or near the eyes

traditional_use.practice: Neem leaves or neem oil for bites and to keep mosquitoes away
traditional_use.note: Neem is traditionally used against insects. Some small studies suggest a repellent effect, but it is less proven than standard repellents.
traditional_use.safety: Do not rely on neem alone in dengue or malaria season. Patch-test first, and do not use neem oil on babies.

audience_notes.child: Keep children’s nails short and watch for fever in the days after bites during monsoon.
audience_notes.infant: For babies, use nets and covering clothes. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using any repellent or cream.

options.label: No, just a local itchy bump
Yes
options.reason: This can be a severe allergic reaction. Call 112 now.

clarify.text: Any fever since the bites?

options.label: Yes, fever or body ache
options.reason: Fever after mosquito bites can signal dengue or malaria. See a doctor for testing.

title: Bee or wasp sting
problem: A painful sting from a bee, wasp (tatiya) or hornet.
modern_guidance: Remove any sting left in the skin by scraping sideways, wash the area, and apply a cold compress. Watch closely for signs of a severe allergic reaction.
evidence_summary: NHS guidance covers removing the sting, cold compress, and emergency signs of anaphylaxis.
how_to: If the sting is still in the skin, scrape it out sideways with a fingernail or card edge. Do not squeeze it with fingers.
Wash the area with soap and water.
Hold a cold compress on it for at least 10 minutes. Raise the area if swollen.
Keep watching for any breathing or swelling problems for the next hour.
what_to_avoid: Do not squeeze the sting with tweezers or fingers.
Do not scratch.
Do not apply kerosene or chemicals.
watch_for: Swelling spreading over a larger area over a day or two
Signs of infection
contraindications: Anyone with a known sting allergy should follow their doctor’s emergency plan.
red_flags: Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat
Difficulty breathing, wheezing or a tight throat
Dizziness, fainting, or a fast heartbeat
Many stings at once, or a sting inside the mouth or throat
when_to_seek_help: Large swelling that spreads a lot
Signs of infection
Known allergy to stings

Yes
options.reason: This can be anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction. Call 112 now.

clarify.text: How many stings, and where?

options.label: One or a few on the skin
Many stings, or inside the mouth or throat
options.reason: Many stings or stings in the mouth need emergency care.

title: Minor sprain or twisted ankle
problem: A twisted ankle, wrist or knee with pain and some swelling, where you can still move it.
modern_guidance: For the first 2–3 days, follow PRICE: Protect, Rest, Ice (wrapped), Compression, Elevation. Most sprains feel better within 2 weeks.
evidence_summary: PRICE is the NHS-recommended self-care approach for sprains and strains in the first 2–3 days.
how_to: Protect: support the joint, e.g. with a supportive shoe.
Rest: stop the activity and avoid putting weight on it.
Ice: a cold pack or frozen peas in a cloth for up to 20 minutes every 2–3 hours.
Compression: a bandage for support during the day (not too tight).
Elevate: keep it raised on a pillow when you can.
Once you can move it without much pain, keep it gently moving so it does not stiffen.
what_to_avoid: For the first couple of days avoid heat (hot baths, heat packs), alcohol and massage.
Avoid strenuous exercise like running for several weeks.
watch_for: Pain or swelling getting worse
No improvement after a few days
red_flags: Cannot put any weight on it or walk more than a few steps
The joint looks deformed or out of place
Heard a crack or snap at the time of injury
Numbness, tingling, or the skin below turns pale or cold
Fever or feeling hot and shivery with the swelling
when_to_seek_help: It is very painful or getting worse
Large or worsening swelling or bruising
It is not improving after treating it yourself

traditional_use.practice: Hot haldi-chuna (turmeric and lime) lep or hot oil massage right after a sprain
traditional_use.note: Very common in Indian homes. There is no good evidence it speeds healing.
traditional_use.safety: Heat and massage in the first 2 days may increase swelling. Lime (chuna) can burn skin. Prefer a cold pack early on.

clarify.text: Can you put weight on it or use it a little?

options.label: No, or it looks out of shape
options.reason: This could be a fracture or dislocation. Get it checked today.

title: Nosebleed
problem: Bleeding from the nose, often from dry air, heat, nose picking or blowing hard.
age_range: All ages (under 2s should see a doctor)
modern_guidance: Sit down, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils for 10–15 minutes while breathing through the mouth.
evidence_summary: The lean-forward-and-pinch method is NHS guidance. Ice on the bridge of the nose may help but evidence is weak.
how_to: Sit down and lean forward, with the head tilted forward and mouth open.
Pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils for 10–15 minutes without letting go.
Breathe through your mouth and spit out any blood.
Optional: a cold pack on the top of the nose.
For 24 hours after, avoid blowing or picking the nose, hot drinks, alcohol and heavy lifting.
what_to_avoid: Do not tilt the head back (blood runs down the throat).
Do not lie flat.
Do not stuff cotton deep into the nose.
watch_for: Nosebleeds that keep coming back
Unusual tiredness or paleness
contraindications: People on blood thinners like warfarin should seek advice for any nosebleed.
red_flags: Bleeding longer than 10–15 minutes despite pinching
Heavy bleeding or swallowing a lot of blood causing vomiting
Nosebleed after a blow to the head
Feeling weak, dizzy or having trouble breathing
when_to_seek_help: Nosebleeds happen regularly
A child under 2 has a nosebleed
You take blood-thinning medicine

traditional_use.practice: Tilting the head back, or pouring cold water on the head
traditional_use.note: Tilting back is a common instinct, but guidance is to lean forward.
traditional_use.safety: Tilting back makes you swallow blood, which can cause vomiting and hides how much you are bleeding.

not_for.reason: A nosebleed in a child under 2 should be checked by a doctor.

clarify.text: Has it stopped after 10–15 minutes of pinching?

options.label: Yes, or I have not tried yet
No, still bleeding heavily
options.reason: Bleeding over 15 minutes needs emergency care.

options.label: Yes
options.reason: A nosebleed after a head injury needs emergency assessment.

title: Muscle soreness after activity
situation_label: Muscle soreness after exercise or work
problem: Aching, stiff muscles a day or two after exercise, a long walk, or heavy housework.
modern_guidance: This usually eases on its own in a few days. Gentle movement, stretching, rest and fluids help. Build up activity gradually.
evidence_summary: Delayed muscle soreness is common and self-limiting. Evidence for any specific remedy (massage, stretching, heat) speeding recovery is modest.
how_to: Keep moving gently: a light walk helps more than complete rest.
Gentle stretching within comfort.
A warm bath or a wrapped hot water bottle can ease stiffness (not for fresh injuries with swelling).
Drink enough water and sleep well.
Next time, warm up first and increase effort gradually.
what_to_avoid: Do not push through sharp or sudden pain.
Do not use heat on a fresh injury with swelling.
watch_for: Pain that does not ease after a week
Swelling in one spot
red_flags: Very dark (cola-coloured) urine after hard exercise
Severe muscle pain with weakness or swelling
Chest pain, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back
when_to_seek_help: Pain lasts more than a week or is getting worse
You felt a sudden pop or sharp pain during activity

traditional_use.practice: Warm sarson (mustard) oil massage for sore muscles
traditional_use.note: Common in many Indian homes. Massage in general may ease soreness for some people; evidence for the oil itself is limited.
traditional_use.safety: Use warm, not hot, oil. Mustard oil can irritate some skin. Not for babies’ faces, broken skin or fresh swollen injuries.

source.title: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64
source.supports: Breaking up long periods of sitting; weekly activity targets.

title: Sore throat
problem: Scratchy, painful throat, often with a cold. Usually gets better within a week.
age_range: All ages (salt-water gargle for adults and older children only)
modern_guidance: Rest, drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, and (for adults) gargle with warm salty water. Most sore throats clear up within a week.
evidence_summary: NHS self-care advice for sore throat: fluids, soft foods, rest, salt-water gargles for adults. Antibiotics are usually not needed.
how_to: Drink plenty of water and warm (not hot) fluids.
Adults: gargle with half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, then spit it out.
Eat cool or soft foods.
Rest, and avoid smoke and smoky kitchens.
A pharmacist can suggest lozenges or pain relief suitable for you.
what_to_avoid: Children should not gargle salt water.
Do not give young children hard sweets or anything small and hard (choking risk).
Do not ask for antibiotics for an ordinary sore throat: they usually do not help.
watch_for: Not improving after a week
High temperature, or feeling hot and shivery
Signs of dehydration: peeing less, dark urine
red_flags: Difficulty breathing
Unable to swallow, or drooling
A high-pitched sound when breathing in
Severe symptoms that are getting worse quickly
when_to_seek_help: Not better after a week
Sore throats happen often
A child under 5 needs help for a sore throat
A lump in the neck or a mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks
Weakened immune system (e.g. diabetes, chemotherapy)

traditional_use.practice: Haldi doodh (turmeric milk) for a sore throat
traditional_use.note: A comforting household drink. Warm drinks can soothe; there is no strong evidence that turmeric itself treats sore throats.
traditional_use.safety: Fine as a warm drink for most people. Serve warm, not hot, to children.

traditional_use.practice: Namak ke paani se garare (salt-water gargle)
traditional_use.note: Recommended by NHS guidance for adults to soothe a sore throat.
traditional_use.safety: Not for children. Spit it out, do not swallow.

traditional_use.practice: Adrak-tulsi-shahad (ginger, tulsi, honey) kadha
traditional_use.note: Warm drinks and honey may soothe the throat. Evidence for tulsi and ginger specifically for sore throat is limited.
traditional_use.safety: No honey for babies under 1 year. Keep it warm, not scalding.

audience_notes.child: No salt-water gargles for children. Get advice for a child under 5 with a sore throat.
audience_notes.infant: For babies with a sore throat or poor feeding, speak to a doctor.

not_for.reason: Babies with a sore throat or who are not feeding well should be seen by a doctor.

options.label: Yes, high fever or feeling very unwell

title: Mild cough
problem: A cough, often with a cold. Most coughs clear up within 3–4 weeks.
modern_guidance: Rest and drink plenty of fluids. For adults and children over 1, warm water with lemon and honey may ease the cough.
evidence_summary: NHS advice: rest and fluids. Honey and lemon may help, though evidence is limited. Paediatric guidance supports honey for children aged 1 and older.

If there is vomiting or diarrhoea, use ORS made up exactly as the packet says.
Rest in a cool place.
Keep breastfeeding or formula feeding babies as usual.

title: Monsoon mosquito protection
problem: Protecting the family from mosquitoes that spread dengue and malaria during and after the rains.
modern_guidance: Stop mosquitoes breeding by emptying and covering stored water weekly, and prevent bites with covering clothes, nets, screens and repellents.
evidence_summary: WHO dengue guidance: cover, empty and clean domestic water containers weekly; use clothing, nets, screens and repellents containing DEET, picaridin or IR3535.
how_to: Once a week, empty and scrub coolers, flower-pot trays, buckets, tyres and anything holding water.
Cover water tanks and stored water.
Wear long sleeves and full pants, especially at dawn and dusk (dengue mosquitoes also bite in the day).
Sleep under a mosquito net, including for daytime naps for babies.
Use window screens and a repellent containing DEET, picaridin or IR3535, following the label for age.
what_to_avoid: Letting water collect in coolers, pots and terraces.
Burning coils in closed rooms with children or people with asthma.
watch_for: Fever, severe body ache, pain behind the eyes, rash in the week after bites
contraindications: Check repellent labels for age limits before using on babies and young children.
red_flags: Fever with severe tummy pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool
Fever with extreme tiredness, restlessness or fast breathing
when_to_seek_help: Any fever during dengue/malaria season: see a doctor for testing
Do not self-medicate a fever with ibuprofen or aspirin during dengue season: ask a doctor

traditional_use.practice: Neem leaf smoke or neem oil to keep mosquitoes away
traditional_use.note: Neem has some repellent activity in small studies, but is less proven than standard repellents.
traditional_use.safety: Smoke irritates lungs, especially for children and people with asthma. Use nets and screens as the main protection.

traditional_use.practice: Papaya leaf juice for dengue
traditional_use.note: Widely shared. Some small studies exist, but it is not a treatment for dengue.
traditional_use.safety: Never delay seeing a doctor for fever in dengue season.

source.title: Dengue and severe dengue (fact sheet)
source.supports: Covering skin, nets, repellents (DEET, picaridin, IR3535), emptying stored water weekly.

title: Winter dry skin
problem: Dry, rough, flaky or itchy skin, cracked heels or chapped lips in winter.
modern_guidance: Keep baths short and warm (not hot), pat dry, and apply a moisturising cream or ointment within minutes of bathing. Use gentle, fragrance-free products.
evidence_summary: American Academy of Dermatology tips: short warm showers, moisturise right after, ointments or creams, gentle fragrance-free products, a humidifier.
how_to: Limit baths to 5–10 minutes with warm, not hot, water.
Pat skin dry gently with a towel.
Apply moisturiser within a few minutes of bathing, while skin is still slightly damp.
Ointments and creams work better than lotions for very dry skin.
Use lip balm or petroleum jelly on lips.
Choose gentle, fragrance-free soap and moisturiser.
what_to_avoid: Very hot water baths.
Harsh or strongly perfumed soaps.
Scratching dry patches.
watch_for: Cracks that bleed or become red and sore
Itching that disturbs sleep
red_flags: Red, hot, swollen skin with fever (possible infection)
Widespread rash with blisters
when_to_seek_help: No improvement after a couple of weeks
Intense itching or cracking and bleeding
Signs of infection

traditional_use.practice: Coconut oil or sarson (mustard) oil massage before bath
traditional_use.note: Plant oils can help seal moisture into skin. Coconut oil is a common moisturiser.
traditional_use.safety: Mustard oil can irritate sensitive skin and is not advised on babies’ faces. Patch-test first.

traditional_use.practice: Malai (milk cream) or ghee on chapped lips
traditional_use.note: Traditional and gentle, but not better than a plain lip balm or petroleum jelly.
traditional_use.safety: Usually harmless. Avoid if it causes irritation.

source.title: Dermatologists' top tips for relieving dry skin
source.supports: Short warm showers, moisturise straight after, humidifier, gentle products.

title: Screen fatigue and tired eyes
problem: Dry, tired, aching eyes or blurred vision after long hours on a laptop or phone.
modern_guidance: Blink often, look up and into the distance regularly, sit about an arm’s length from the screen, and reduce glare. Digital eye strain is uncomfortable but does not permanently damage eyes.
evidence_summary: American Academy of Ophthalmology: screen use does not permanently damage eyes; blinking, breaks, screen distance and glare control help.
how_to: Make a habit of blinking: we blink much less while looking at screens.
Every so often, look up and at something far away for a little while.
Sit about 25 inches (an arm’s length) from the screen, with the screen slightly below eye level.
Reduce glare: adjust brightness to match the room, avoid a bright window behind the screen.
A pharmacist can suggest lubricating eye drops for dryness.
what_to_avoid: Using screens in a dark room.
Rubbing eyes.
watch_for: Headaches or blurred vision that continue after screen time
Needing to hold things very close or very far to read
red_flags: Sudden loss of vision
Eye pain with redness and light sensitivity
Flashes of light or a curtain over vision
when_to_seek_help: Blurred vision that does not clear with rest: get an eye test
A child squinting or holding screens very close

traditional_use.practice: Rose water (gulab jal) or cucumber on tired eyes
traditional_use.note: May feel refreshing. Not a treatment for eye strain.
traditional_use.safety: Do not put non-sterile liquids into the eyes. Use only on closed eyelids.

source.title: Computers, Digital Devices, and Eye Strain
source.supports: Blink more, look up and into the distance regularly, sit about an arm’s length from the screen, reduce glare.

title: Poor sleep
problem: Trouble falling asleep, waking up at night, or not feeling rested, for a few nights or weeks.
modern_guidance: Keep regular sleep and wake times, wind down for an hour before bed without screens, keep the room dark, quiet and cool, and limit caffeine and heavy meals in the evening.
evidence_summary: NHS guidance on sleep and on tiredness: regular routines, a restful bedroom, avoiding screens, caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals before bed.
how_to: Get up at the same time every day, even after a bad night.
Wind down for an hour before bed: dim lights, read, listen to music, or try slow breathing.
Keep the room dark, quiet and not too warm.
Stop caffeine (tea, coffee, cola) by mid-afternoon.
Avoid heavy meals, exercise and alcohol in the couple of hours before bed.
If you cannot sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm, then return to bed.
what_to_avoid: Screens in bed.
Long daytime naps.
Using alcohol as a sleep aid.
Buying sleeping pills without a doctor.
watch_for: Sleep problems lasting weeks
Low mood, worry or stress keeping you awake
red_flags: Loud snoring with gasping or choking during sleep
Thoughts of self-harm or hopelessness
when_to_seek_help: Poor sleep for several weeks despite changes
It affects daily life, work or driving
Snoring with gasping or pauses in breathing

traditional_use.practice: Warm milk, or a foot massage with oil (padabhyanga), before bed
traditional_use.note: Part of calming bedtime routines in many homes. A relaxing routine helps sleep; the specific remedy is not proven.
traditional_use.safety: Generally harmless.

traditional_use.practice: Pranayama / slow breathing before sleep
traditional_use.note: Slow, relaxed breathing is a common relaxation technique that may help you wind down.
traditional_use.safety: Keep it gentle. Stop if you feel dizzy.

title: Stiff neck from desk work or sleeping
problem: A stiff, sore neck after sleeping awkwardly or long hours at a desk or phone.
modern_guidance: Keep the neck gently moving, use heat or cold packs, sit upright, and use a low firm pillow. Most neck pain eases within a few weeks.
evidence_summary: NHS neck pain guidance: keep moving, heat or cold packs, posture, pillow height.
how_to: Keep your neck moving gently. Try slow neck turns and tilts within comfort.
Cold pack (frozen peas in a towel) for 5 minutes, 3 times a day, or a wrapped hot water bottle for 20 minutes, 2–3 times a day.
Sit upright, roll your shoulders back gently, and bring the screen to eye level.
Take a break from the same position every 30–60 minutes.
Use a low, firm pillow; avoid sleeping on your front.
what_to_avoid: Wearing a neck collar unless a doctor advises.
Driving or cycling if you cannot turn your head.
watch_for: Pins and needles or weakness in the arm
Pain not easing after a few weeks
red_flags: Stiff neck with fever and a headache, or bright light hurting the eyes
Neck pain after a fall or accident
Numbness or weakness in arms or legs, or loss of bladder control
when_to_seek_help: Pain or stiffness lasting more than a few weeks
Painkillers are not helping
Other symptoms like pins and needles

title: Heat rash (ghamoriyan) and minor skin irritation
situation_label: Heat rash or minor skin irritation
problem: Small, itchy, prickly red or skin-coloured spots in hot, sweaty weather, often on the neck, back or chest.
modern_guidance: Keep the skin cool so it does not sweat: loose cotton clothes, light bedding, cool baths and plenty of fluids. Heat rash usually settles on its own in a few days.
evidence_summary: NHS guidance on heat rash: keep skin cool, cold compress, pat instead of scratching, avoid perfumed products; a pharmacist can suggest treatments.
how_to: Wear loose cotton clothing and use light bedding.
Take cool baths or showers.
Drink plenty of fluids.
For itching: a damp cloth or wrapped ice pack for up to 20 minutes.
Tap or pat the skin instead of scratching.
A pharmacist can suggest calamine lotion or other treatments suitable for the person’s age.
what_to_avoid: Perfumed soaps, shower gels and creams.
Thick oils or heavy creams that block sweat.
Hydrocortisone cream for children under 10 without a doctor’s advice.
watch_for: Rash not improving after a few days
Spots becoming painful, filled with pus, or spreading
red_flags: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, especially with fever
Rash with swelling of the face or lips, or trouble breathing
A baby with a rash who is unwell, floppy, or has a high temperature
when_to_seek_help: Not improving after a few days
A baby has a rash and you are worried
Signs of infection

traditional_use.practice: Prickly heat powder, multani mitti or sandalwood (chandan) paste
traditional_use.note: Cooling pastes and powders are traditional in Indian summers. Keeping skin cool and dry is what the evidence supports.
traditional_use.safety: Avoid talc near a baby’s face (breathing it in). Stop anything that stings or worsens the rash.

audience_notes.infant: Babies get heat rash easily because they cannot control temperature well. Dress them lightly. If a baby with a rash seems unwell, see a doctor.

clarify.text: Does the rash fade when you press a clear glass against it? Any fever?

options.reason: A rash that does not fade under a glass, especially with fever, needs emergency care.
